October sixth, nineteen ninety-seven. Orlando, Florida.
At a technology conference, someone asks Michael Dell, one of the most powerful men in the computer business, a simple question.
What would he do with Apple?
His answer becomes one of the most famous lines in tech history.
I'd shut it down, and give the money back to the shareholders.
It wasn't a crazy thing to say.
That year, Apple lost a billion dollars.
Its share of the world's computer market had fallen to about three percent.
Its co-founder had been gone for twelve years, and had only just come back.
Ten years later, Apple would earn three and a half billion dollars, in a single year.
So what actually changed? And how much of it was one man?
This is Empire Stories.
Jobs' answer was not to add. It was to subtract.
So he cut. Roughly seventy percent of Apple's products were cancelled, including the Newton handheld.
Then, at a whiteboard, he drew a grid. Two columns: Consumer, and Pro. Two rows: Desktop, and Portable.
Four boxes. Four products.
And one box was still empty. A computer for ordinary people, at home.
On May sixth, nineteen ninety-eight, Jobs filled it.
The iMac looked like no other computer on the market. An all-in-one machine in translucent blue-green plastic, with a handle on top.
It made bold bets too. No floppy disk drive. New U S B ports, instead of Apple's old connectors.
It went on sale on August fifteenth, nineteen ninety-eight, for twelve hundred and ninety-nine dollars.
In its first six weeks, Apple shipped two hundred and seventy-eight thousand iMacs.
When fiscal nineteen ninety-eight closed, Apple reported a profit of three hundred and nine million dollars. Its first profitable year, since nineteen ninety-five.
